theory.what: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer conceptual framework that standardizes how network communication works. Each layer has a specific function.
theory.why: Understanding the OSI model is fundamental because it provides a common language for troubleshooting. When something breaks, you can isolate which layer is failing — is it a physical cable issue (Layer 1), a switching problem (Layer 2), a routing issue (Layer 3), or an application bug (Layer 7)?
theory.how:
Data flows down the stack on the sender (encapsulation) and up the stack on the receiver (de-encapsulation). Each layer adds its own header:

7. Application — HTTP, DNS, SMTP
6. Presentation — Encryption, compression
5. Session — Session management
4. Transport — TCP/UDP, ports
3. Network — IP addressing, routing
2. Data Link — MAC addresses, switching
1. Physical — Cables, signals, bits
theory.when: Use the OSI model when troubleshooting any network issue. Start from Layer 1 (is the cable plugged in?) and work up, or start from Layer 7 (is the application configured correctly?) and work down.
key_concepts: Each layer serves the layer above it
theory.configuration: N/A — conceptual model, not a configurable protocol
troubleshooting: Layer 1: Check cables, link lights, interface status
Layer 2: Check MAC table, ARP, VLAN assignment
Layer 3: Check IP config, routing table, ping
Layer 4: Check port connectivity, firewall rules
Layer 7: Check application logs, DNS resolution

theory.what: The TCP/IP model is a 4-layer practical networking model that the internet actually uses. It's simpler than OSI and maps directly to real protocols.
theory.why: While OSI is theoretical, TCP/IP is what actually runs the internet. Every packet you send uses this model. Understanding it means understanding how the internet works at every level.
theory.how:
4 Layers:
1. Network Access (Link) — Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP
2. Internet — IP, ICMP, routing
3. Transport — TCP, UDP
4. Application — HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP

Data flows: Application creates data → Transport segments it → Internet adds IP addressing → Network Access frames it for the wire.
theory.when: Use TCP/IP when discussing real-world networking. OSI is for conceptual understanding; TCP/IP is for implementation.

theory.what: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller, more manageable sub-networks. Each subnet has its own network address, broadcast address, and usable host range.
theory.why: Without subnetting, you'd have one massive broadcast domain. Subnetting reduces broadcast traffic, improves security (segments can be isolated), enables efficient IP allocation, and is required for routing between networks.
theory.how:
Subnetting works by borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address to create subnet bits.

Example: 192.168.1.0/24 → split into 4 subnets:
- 192.168.1.0/26 (hosts: .1-.62, broadcast: .63)
- 192.168.1.64/26 (hosts: .65-.126, broadcast: .127)
- 192.168.1.128/26 (hosts: .129-.190, broadcast: .191)
- 192.168.1.192/26 (hosts: .193-.254, broadcast: .255)

Formula: 2^n subnets, 2^h - 2 hosts (n=subnet bits, h=host bits)
theory.when: Subnet when you need to: separate departments, create VLANs, optimize routing, meet security requirements, or efficiently allocate IP space.
theory.configuration:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.192
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.65 255.255.255.192
troubleshooting: Hosts can't communicate? Check if they're on the same subnet
Wrong subnet mask = wrong broadcast domain

theory.what: DNS translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into IP addresses (142.250.80.46). It's the phone book of the internet.
theory.why: Humans remember names, computers use numbers. DNS bridges this gap. Without DNS, you'd need to memorize IP addresses for every website. DNS also enables load balancing, failover, and service discovery.
theory.how:
DNS resolution process:
1. User types google.com
2. Browser checks local cache
3. OS checks hosts file, then local DNS cache
4. Query goes to recursive resolver (ISP or 8.8.8.8)
5. Resolver queries root servers → .com TLD → google.com authoritative NS
6. Authoritative server returns IP
7. Result cached at each level (TTL)

Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (nameserver), TXT (text), SOA (authority)
theory.when: DNS is involved in virtually every network connection. Troubleshoot DNS when: websites don't load but IP works, email delivery fails, services can't find each other.
theory.configuration:
# Linux DNS config
cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 8.8.4.4

# Windows
netsh interface ip set dns "Ethernet" static 8.8.8.8
